source.title: Botafogo wide free kick: avoiding the last-defender block

situation.outcome: The wider starting position and open body orientation help the defender negotiate the blocking action
situation.human_observation: This clip is presented as one of four defensive counter-strategies to the last-defender blocking tactic described elsewhere in the article (see A-0007, PSG vs Inter Miami). The article frames it as a subtler, more proactive adjustment compared to simply shifting the whole line towards the far post, which can leave the front-post zone exposed instead. The Botafogo clip specifically highlights two adjustments from the last defender: an open body orientation, which helps him maintain visual contact with the attacker on his blindside, and starting a few steps wider from the rest of the line, which gives him more room to negotiate/avoid the block when it comes.
situation.priority_problem: How the last defender in a zonal line can individually protect himself against a blocking action (as exploited in cases like PSG vs Inter Miami) through body positioning and starting position alone, without requiring a wholesale change to the team's defensive shape or line height.
visible_evidence: The last defender in Botafogo's zonal line adopts an open body orientation rather than a closed one.
This open orientation allows him to keep visual contact with both the ball and the attacker approaching from his blindside.
The same defender starts his position a few steps wider than the rest of the zonal line.
This wider starting position gives him additional room/space to negotiate or avoid the blocking action when an attacker attempts it.

coaching.objective: Enable the last defender in a zonal free-kick line to individually resist blocking actions through open body orientation and a wider starting position, preserving blindside awareness and manoeuvring room without needing to alter the team's overall defensive shape or line height.
coaching.practice_design: Individual/unit defending practice for the last defender in a zonal wide-free-kick line: rehearse holding an open body shape (rather than square-on/closed to the play) so the defender can track both the ball and any blindside attacker simultaneously. Pair this with a starting position a few steps wider than the rest of the zonal line, giving room to step around or resist an incoming screen/block. Run repeated reps against an attacker attempting a blocking run so the defender practises recognising the block early (due to better visual contact) and adjusting his body/footwork to get past it, rather than being caught passively.
success_cues: Last defender maintains visual contact with the blindside attacker throughout the delivery, not just the ball.
Defender's starting position is visibly wider than the rest of the zonal line, without compromising overall line coverage.
Defender recognises an incoming block early enough to adjust his body position or footwork.
Defender is able to negotiate around or resist the block rather than being pinned/screened out of the play.
The far-post zone remains covered without requiring the whole line to shift or drop, preserving front-post coverage as well.

limitations: The article gives this example relatively brief treatment (two sentences) compared to the detailed PSG/Inter Miami breakdown in A-0007; some contextual detail (e.g. Botafogo's opponent, match context, outcome of the specific free kick) is not stated in the source text.
